content.text: To make assessment valid, reliable and fair, so that it guides teaching, improves student learning and gives accurate feedback to students and parents. It also keeps integrity across both Cambridge and Indonesian assessment requirements.

Eduversal schools use a balanced approach to assessment with three parts. Assessment FOR Learning is formative assessment that supports teaching. Assessment AS Learning is students reflecting on their own learning and setting goals. Assessment OF Learning is summative assessment that measures achievement against standards.

All assessments are based on standards, fair and transparent. Students receive timely feedback that they can act on.
content.title: Core Beliefs

items: Assessment during learning to find needs, adjust teaching and give feedback
Purpose: Improve learning as it happens, not just measure it
Students reflect on their own learning, set goals and track their progress
Purpose: Develop metacognition and self-regulation
Assessment at the end of a unit, term or course to measure achievement against standards
Purpose: Report what students can do, confirm mastery and guide decisions (promotion, graduation)
All assessments are aligned to clear learning objectives (Cambridge, Indonesian CP – Capaian Pembelajaran – and SLOs)
Students are assessed against standards, not against each other (criterion-referenced, not norm-referenced)
Assessments are accessible to all students, with accommodations for EAL (English as an Additional Language) and SEN (Special Educational Needs) students as needed
Several kinds of evidence are used (tests, projects, presentations, portfolios), not just exams
Bias is kept as low as possible: assessments respect students' cultures, use suitable language and include diverse examples
Assessment criteria (rubrics, mark schemes) are shared with students before the assessment.
Students understand what good-quality work looks like.
Grades are based on evidence, not on effort or behavior. Character and effort are reported separately.
Feedback is given promptly (within 1-2 weeks for major assessments)
Feedback is specific, helpful and practical: it tells students what to improve and how
Students get chances to use feedback (revisions, and re-assessments when appropriate)
Assessment data guides teaching decisions (re-teach, differentiate or accelerate)
Teachers work together to analyze data and improve practice in PLCs (Professional Learning Communities)

content.title: Where an examination clashes with an EASE Week
content.text:
If a Cambridge examination falls in the same week as a Synchronized Test, the Cambridge examination replaces the Synchronized Test. This applies to the grades and subjects sitting the Cambridge examination, as shown in the live EASE Schedule. Other grades and subjects sit the Synchronized Test as scheduled. If a national examination falls in an EASE Week, the grades sitting it move the EASE assessment to the next available week. Grades not sitting it continue as scheduled. Two such overlaps occur in the sample calendar.

EASE Week 4 (Semester 2, Week 19, 10-14 May) falls inside the Cambridge external examination window at Weeks 18-20. Grade 10 (IGCSE) and Grade 12 (A Level continuers) sit the May/June series. For these grades, the Cambridge examinations replace the Synchronized Test in the subjects where they sit Cambridge examinations. Other grades and subjects sit the Synchronized Test as scheduled. EASE Week 1 (Semester 1, Week 12, 28 Sep - 4 Oct) falls at the same time as ANBK where a school is scheduled for it. ANBK is Asesmen Nasional Berbasis Komputer, the national computer-based assessment. In the sample year, this affects Grades 5, 8 and 11.

The rule is stated here instead of a fixed alternative date, because the Cambridge window moves each series. A fixed replacement week would be wrong the following year. Each year, the live EASE Schedule records which grade and subject combinations a Cambridge examination replaces.

content.text: Purpose: Give regular feedback during learning, so students can improve before summative assessments.

items: Process: At the end of the lesson, students write a short response on an index card or digital form
Example: "Write 3 things you learned today, 2 questions you still have, 1 thing you'll practice tonight"
Use: The teacher reviews the responses, finds misunderstandings and adjusts the next lesson
Frequency: 2-3 times per week
Process: Ask a question → students think alone (1 min) → discuss with a partner (2 min) → share with the class
Use: Checks understanding, encourages participation and finds gaps as they appear
Frequency: Multiple times per lesson
Process: Teacher asks "How confident are you with this concept?" → Students signal (thumb up = confident, sideways = somewhat, down = need help) or vote via app (Kahoot, Mentimeter, Google Forms)
Use: A quick check of the whole class's understanding; the teacher then plans different next steps for different students
Frequency: 1-2 times per lesson
Process: Students hand in a draft essay or project → the teacher or a peer gives feedback using a rubric → students revise before final submission
Use: Improves the final work and teaches students to assess themselves and give helpful feedback
Frequency: For major writing assignments and projects
Process: Teacher observes students during independent work, group activities and discussions → records notes on student understanding, skills and behaviors
Use: Guides teaching and identifies students who need support or extension
Frequency: Ongoing; teachers keep notes on each student
Process: Students assess their own work against a rubric or criteria, identify strengths and areas for growth, and set goals
Use: Develops metacognition (thinking about one's own learning) and ownership of learning
Frequency: After major assessments and at the end of a unit
Specific: "Your thesis statement clearly states your argument" (not just "Good job")
Actionable: "To improve, add evidence from the text to support your claim in paragraph 2"

Timely: Given while the student is still working on the topic or skill. Quick checks (exit tickets, short quizzes) get feedback within 24-48 hours; larger tasks get it within a time that matches the size of the task.
Balanced: Acknowledge strengths AND identify areas for growth
Goal-Oriented: Linked to learning objectives and the student's own goals
Written comments: On student work (margins, end comments)
Rubrics: Checked indicators with brief comments
Verbal feedback: During conferences, in-class check-ins
Audio/Video feedback: Recorded comments (especially useful for detailed feedback on essays or projects)
Peer feedback: Structured peer review using protocols or rubrics

Best for: Assessing recall of knowledge, understanding and analysis
Match questions to learning objectives (test what was taught)
Include a range of difficulty (easy to challenging)
Use Bloom's Taxonomy levels: not just recall, but also application, analysis, synthesis and evaluation
Clear instructions and adequate time

Best for: Assessing application, creativity, practical skills, communication
Authentic (real-world relevance)
Clear task description and rubric
Chances for planning, practice and feedback before the final performance

Checkpoints along the way (proposal, outline, draft, final)
A rubric that covers both the process (research, effort, time management) and the product (quality, accuracy, presentation)
Balance each student's own responsibility with teamwork (for group projects)

content.text: Before giving a summative assessment, teachers check:

items: Alignment: All questions and tasks match the content taught and the learning objectives
Coverage: The assessment covers the whole unit (not just one topic)
Validity: The assessment measures what it is meant to measure (e.g., a math test assesses math, not just reading comprehension of word problems)
Reliability: The assessment would give the same results if given again or marked by a different teacher (clear rubric, objective criteria)
Fairness: No bias; accessible to all students, with appropriate accommodations
Clarity: Instructions clear, questions unambiguous
Time: Enough time for students to finish (not rushed)
Rubric/Mark Scheme: Prepared in advance and shared with students

content.text:
Moderation is the process in which teachers review student work together. It makes sure that marking is fair, accurate and consistent with agreed standards across teachers, classes and time. Moderation protects the integrity of assessment. It makes sure that all students are graded against the same expectations.

Purpose: Make marking consistent and fair. This matters most for subjective assessments (essays, projects, performance tasks) and for subjects with teacher-assessed components (Cambridge coursework).
Moderation: A process in which teachers review and discuss student work together. It makes sure their marking matches the standards and is consistent across classes, teachers and time.
content.title: What is Moderation?
1. Pre-Assessment Standardization (Before Marking)
content.text:
When: Before teachers start marking a major assessment (e.g., end-of-term essays, IGCSE coursework)

Process:

items: Select anchor samples: Choose 3-5 pieces of student work that show a range of quality (high, medium, low)
Independent marking: Each teacher marks anchor samples independently using rubric
Compare marks: Teachers share their marks and reasoning
Discuss differences: If marks differ significantly (>10%), discuss how each teacher reads the rubric and reach a shared understanding
Reach consensus: Agree on marks for the anchor samples; these become the benchmark

content.text: Outcome: Teachers agree on the standards before marking the full class set

content.title: 2. During-Marking Moderation (Spot Checks)
content.text:
When: While marking is underway (halfway through marking the class set)

Process:

items: Sample exchange: Teachers exchange 5-10 scripts with a colleague who teaches the same subject and grade
Blind re-mark: The colleague re-marks the scripts without seeing the original marks
Compare: If marks are within 5-10%, consistency is confirmed; if the difference is > 10%, discuss and adjust
Adjust if needed: If the marking shows a pattern (e.g., a teacher is always too harsh or too lenient), adjust marks for all students

content.title: 3. Post-Marking Moderation (Final Review)
content.text:
When: After all marking is complete, before grades are finalized

Process:

items: Data review: The HOD (Head of Department) or Academic Coordinator reviews the grade distribution (how many A, B, C, etc.)
Check for anomalies: If one class has all A's and another has all C's on the same assessment → investigate
Sample review: The HOD reviews a sample of marked work from each teacher
Feedback to teachers: If there are concerns (inconsistent marking, marking that is too harsh or too lenient, rubric misapplied), give feedback and ask for adjustments

content.text: Outcome: Confidence that grades are fair, accurate, consistent

Requirement: Some Cambridge subjects have teacher-assessed coursework (e.g., Art & Design portfolio, Science practical skills). For these subjects, schools must carry out internal moderation before submitting marks to Cambridge (Section 3.13). Process:

steps: Teacher assesses student work using Cambridge mark schemes
Internal moderation: The HOD or an experienced colleague reviews a sample (highest, middle and lowest achieving students)
Adjust marks if needed: Make sure marks match Cambridge standards
Submit marks to Cambridge: Via Cambridge International Direct
External moderation by Cambridge: Cambridge selects a sample to review. If it finds a discrepancy, it may adjust the school's marks up or down for all students.

items: Internal moderation meeting notes (dates, participants, samples reviewed, decisions)
Moderation cover sheets (record of marks before and after moderation)
Anchor samples with marks and annotations
External moderation feedback from Cambridge (if applicable)

content.text:
Academic grades show student achievement against curriculum standards.

Purely subjective character and effort indicators — such as organization, attitude and perseverance — are reported separately. They are not included when academic grades are calculated.

Two categories sit on both sides of this line, and they must not be confused. Class Participation and Homework are reported as character/effort habits on the E/S/N scale below. They are also Gradebook categories with defined academic weights in the Assessment Policy:

Class Participation at every key stage. Homework Average at Grades 7-12 only, where what carries weight is the graded quality of the work, not the completion record.

Primary (Grades 1-6) homework rules are set by the Primary Director's separately issued Primary documents.

Challenge: Eduversal schools report grades for both the Cambridge curriculum (international standards) and Indonesian national subjects (Indonesian standards). The two use different scales and philosophies.

items: Official Cambridge grades: A*, A, B, C, D, E, F, G, U (or 9-1 scale for some subjects)
Given by Cambridge, based on external exam results (and coursework, if applicable)

items.text: School-based grades (during the course, before external exams):
items: Schools use predicted grades (the grade the teacher expects the student to achieve in the final Cambridge exam)
OR percentage or letter grades aligned to the Cambridge published grade boundaries, which are updated each year (not a fixed percentage-to-grade table)
Lower Secondary (Grades 7-8) uses the fixed Eduversal Network Standard conversion below; Primary grading scales are set by the Primary Director's separately issued Primary documents
Percentage (0-100%): Clear, quantitative
Letter grades (A-F): A = Excellent, B = Good, C = Satisfactory, D = Needs Improvement, F = Fail
4 = Exceeds expectations
3 = Meets expectations
2 = Approaching expectations
1 = Below expectations

content.title: Eduversal Network Standard — Percentage to Grade Conversion

items: Use percentage scale (0-100%) for consistency across schools
Conversion to descriptive grades:
Scale: 0-100 (percentage)

Attainment criteria (KKTP - Kriteria Ketercapaian Tujuan Pembelajaran): Each school sets its own criteria for each learning objective. There is no fixed passing number for the whole network. The school decides its criteria and records them in its assessment policy.
90-100 = Sangat Baik (Excellent)
80-89 = Baik (Good)
70-79 = Cukup (Satisfactory)
Below 70 = Kurang (Needs Improvement). Remediation is triggered by the school's own KKTP on a Common Assessment component, not by this band
Separate from subject grades
MB (Mulai Berkembang) - Beginning to Develop
BSH (Berkembang Sesuai Harapan) - Developing as Expected
SAB (Sudah Berkembang) - Well Developed
SB (Sangat Berkembang) - Highly Developed
Each of the 6 Profil Pelajar Pancasila dimensions is rated separately (Beriman, Berkebinekaan Global, Bergotong Royong, Mandiri, Bernalar Kritis, Kreatif)

content.text: Philosophy: Academic grades show achievement against standards. Character/effort grades show habits, behaviors and attitudes. Character/Effort Indicators:

items: Participation: Takes part in class discussions, asks questions, contributes to group work
Homework Completion: Hands in assignments on time, shows effort
Organization: Comes prepared with materials, keeps work neat and organized
Perseverance: Keeps trying when work is difficult, asks for help when needed
Respect: Treats others respectfully, follows classroom norms
E (Excellent): Shows positive habits consistently
S (Satisfactory): Usually shows positive habits
N (Needs Improvement): Shows positive habits inconsistently; an improvement plan is needed
Character/effort grades appear in a separate section of the report card. They are not averaged into the academic GPA.

subsections.title: Use of Assessment Data to Inform Instruction

content.text: Purpose: Assessment is not the end point. It is a tool to improve teaching and learning.
What are PLCs? Professional Learning Communities: teams of teachers (same subject, same grade, or across grades) who meet regularly. They analyze student data, share strategies and improve practice.

items: Teachers bring assessment data (recent quiz, unit test, formative assessments)
Strengths: Which learning objectives did most students master?
Gaps: Which objectives did many students struggle with?
Outliers: Are any students well above or below the class average?
Insufficient instructional time?
Is the concept too abstract?
Language barriers (EAL)?
Prerequisite skills missing?
Assessment unclear or too difficult?
For the whole class: Re-teach the concept in a different way (more visuals, a hands-on activity, a real-world example)
For small groups: Targeted intervention during class (take a small group for reteaching while the others work on their own) or after school
For individuals: One-on-one tutoring, a modified assignment, or referral to EAL/SEN support
Teachers share what worked well (successful lesson, effective assessment, differentiation strategy)
Borrow ideas from colleagues

content.title: 5. Set Goals for Next Meeting (5 min)

items: Commit to trying new strategy
Plan next assessment to monitor progress
Schedule follow-up

content.title: 6. Teacher Professional Development Based on Data
content.text: DTP (Development of Teaching Proficiency): a network-wide professional development program. It addresses gaps found through assessment data, Appraisal results and PLC discussions

items: PLC meeting agendas and notes
Data analysis protocols (templates for reviewing data)
Intervention plans
Evidence of impact (assessment data from before and after the intervention that shows improvement)

content.text: Root Cause: Teaching moved too quickly. Students needed more practice with scaffolded problems before they tried complex multi-step equations

items: Whole Class: Reteach multi-step equations with clear step-by-step modeling; use color-coding to show each step
Small Group: Take 10 students for extra practice during next week's independent work time
Individual: 3 students referred to after-school math support for basic gaps in operations

content.text: Re-Assessment: Quiz given 1 week after intervention
Result: 85% of students now score above 70%, a significant improvement
Next Steps: Continue scaffolding; add more frequent chances to practice; monitor progress closely
Data: Semester 1 EASE writing scores show 40% of Grade 10 students below proficiency in argumentative writing

items: Organizing arguments logically
Providing textual evidence
Analyzing evidence (not just quoting)
Students have limited experience with the argumentative genre
They need explicit teaching in structure and analytical writing
Curriculum Adjustment: Add 2-week unit on argumentative writing before next essay assignment
Model essays (analyze structure, thesis statements, evidence use)
Practice writing thesis statements and topic sentences
Teach "claim-evidence-analysis" paragraph structure
Scaffolding: Provide graphic organizers (essay outline template)
Peer Review: Students exchange drafts and give feedback using the rubric before final submission
EAL Support: Push-in support during writing lessons for EAL students; pre-teach academic vocabulary

content.text: Re-Assessment: Next essay assignment (1 month later)
Result: 70% are now proficient or above; support continues for the other students
Purpose: Build a culture of honesty, original thinking and proper crediting of sources. Prevent academic dishonesty and deal with it when it happens.

items: Plagiarism: Using someone else's words, ideas or work without proper citation (this includes copying from the internet, books or peers)
Cheating: Using materials or help that are not allowed during assessments (cheat sheets, copying answers, using a phone)
Collusion: Working together when this is not allowed (working together on an individual assignment and submitting similar work)
Fabrication: Making up data, sources, or citations
Facilitation: Helping another student cheat (sharing answers, letting someone copy)
AI Misuse: Submitting AI-generated work without saying so, or using AI inappropriately. For example, AI writes the entire essay when the task requires the student's own original writing.
What is copying vs. own work
How to paraphrase (put in own words)
When to give credit (if you learned from someone/something, say where)
Citation styles (MLA, APA, Chicago - depending on subject)
Paraphrasing vs. quoting vs. summarizing
How to integrate sources into writing
When citation is required (direct quotes, paraphrases, statistics, ideas)
Process-based assignments: Require drafts, outlines and research logs (plagiarism is harder when the process is recorded)
Unique prompts: Change essay questions/project topics each year (so students can't copy from previous students)
In-class components: Include in-class writing, presentations or checkpoints (these check that the student understands and can do the work alone)
Authentic tasks: Real-world problems or creative prompts are less likely to have ready-made answers online
Plagiarism detection software: Turnitin, Grammarly Plagiarism Checker, or similar (students submit essays electronically; the software checks them against a database)
Educational use: Show students the similarity report and discuss proper citation (not just punishment)
AI detection tools: GPTZero, Turnitin AI detector (use them carefully; they are not 100% accurate; combine them with other evidence)
Value learning over grades: Stress growth, effort and improvement (this reduces pressure to cheat)
Normalize asking for help: Make it clear that asking a teacher or tutor for help is encouraged (it is not cheating)
Honor code or integrity pledge: Students sign a commitment to honesty at the start of the year

content.text:
If Plagiarism/Cheating Suspected:

Step 1: Gather Evidence

items: Teacher records the concern (suspicious similarity to an online source, a sudden change in writing quality, identical answers to a peer, etc.)
Run plagiarism check or compare work samples
Teacher meets the student privately and shows the evidence
Ask the student to explain (give the benefit of the doubt; it may be a misunderstanding, not intentional dishonesty)
Student may admit or deny

content.text: Step 3: Determine Violation Level and Consequence
Minor Violation (First offense, unintentional, limited scope):

items: Example: Student forgot to cite one source in the bibliography; paraphrased without citation but did not copy word for word
Educational conversation (explain why it is wrong and how to avoid it)
Redo assignment with proper citations
Warning recorded but no grade penalty (or minor penalty, e.g., -10%)
Example: Copied several paragraphs from a website without citation; worked with others inappropriately on an individual assignment
Zero on assignment or reduced grade (e.g., 50% maximum)
Parent notification
Reflection essay or academic integrity workshop
Recorded in student file

content.text: Major Violation (Serious, repeated, or high-stakes assessment):

items: Example: Submitted a fully plagiarized essay; used a phone to cheat on an exam; helped others to cheat
Zero on assignment/exam
Referral to Principal/GM (disciplinary action may include suspension)
Parent meeting
May affect the grade for the course or eligibility for honors
Recorded in the student file; may be noted on the transcript for university applications (depending on how serious it is)
Teacher completes Academic Integrity Incident Report
Includes: Description of violation, evidence, student response, consequence, follow-up plan
Stored in student file and discipline records

content.text: For Cambridge exams or coursework: Follow the procedures in Section 3.10 (must report to Cambridge; Cambridge investigates and decides the sanctions)
content.title: Cambridge-Specific Malpractice

content.text: AI tools may be used to support learning, for example for idea generation, research support, language development and proofreading. However, students must always submit work that shows their own understanding and original thinking. Using AI to produce full answers, essays or solutions and then submitting them as the student’s own work is academic misconduct. Detailed guidelines for acceptable AI use are in Digital Citizenship & AI Appendix B: AI Responsible Use Policy 26-27. Teachers state the permitted AI level on every task. Where a task states no level, the default for submitted work is no AI. Where the task permits it, permitted AI use includes:

items: Brainstorming: Generate topic ideas and outline structures
Grammar/spelling check: Grammarly, spell-checkers for proofreading
Translation support: Translate key terms or phrases to help understanding (EAL students)
Research assistant: Ask AI to explain difficult concepts or suggest resources (but check accuracy)
Writing essays or responses: AI writes content that the student submits as their own work
Solving problems: AI solves math problems, science questions, etc., and the student copies the answers without understanding
Creating projects/presentations: AI generates slides, posters or artwork that the student submits as their own original work

content.text: Guideline: If the assignment assesses students' writing, thinking or problem-solving, AI should not do that work. AI can support the process but not replace the student's own thinking.
Declaration: For major assignments, students sign a statement: "I certify this is my own work. I used [tools/resources] for [purpose]. All AI-generated content is clearly marked and cited."

items: Academic integrity policy (published in student handbook, website)
Signed integrity pledges (start of year)
Lesson plans on citation and integrity
Plagiarism check reports (Turnitin summaries)
Academic integrity incident reports (anonymized summaries for review; individual reports stay confidential)

content.text: Principle: Fair assessment means giving every student the chance to show what they know and can do. This sometimes needs different conditions or formats.
For Students with IEPs or Documented Needs:

items: Extended time (up to 25% meets the needs of most students, e.g. a 90 min test → 112 min; over 25% where difficulties are very significant and persistent – see 8.6)
Frequent breaks (5-10 min break every 30-45 min)
Separate quiet room (minimize distractions)
Small group setting (less anxiety)
Special seating (at the front of the room, away from the window)
Enlarged print (font size 14-18)
Read-aloud (teacher or software reads questions to student)
Simpler language (difficult instructions are reworded, but the content does not change)
Visual aids (graphic organizers, diagrams)
Scribe (the student says the answers aloud and a scribe writes them down)
Word processor (typing instead of handwriting)
Oral response (the student speaks the answers instead of writing them)
Dictation software (speech-to-text)

steps: Identification: A psychologist/specialist assesses the student, and the need is recorded in the IEP (Individual Education Plan)
Approval: The Academic Coordinator/SEN Coordinator approves the accommodations
Implementation: Teachers use the accommodations in all assessments. This covers classroom tests, and Cambridge exams if Cambridge approves them
Documentation: Accommodations are recorded in the student file, and evidence of their use is kept

items: Students choose from a menu of options to show what they have learned
Option A: Written test (multiple choice + short answer)
Option B: Make a 3D cell model with labeled parts, and explain it orally
Option C: Produce video explaining cell structure and function
All options assess the same learning objectives, but they suit different strengths
Same learning objective, different complexity levels
Tier 1 (Approaching): Add/subtract fractions with like denominators
Tier 2 (Meeting): Add/subtract fractions with unlike denominators
Tier 3 (Exceeding): Solve word problems involving multiple operations with fractions
Allow students to choose the format (essay, presentation, poster, video, podcast, etc.) as long as they meet the content requirements
IEP/accommodation documentation
Differentiated assessment examples (choice boards, tiered tasks)
Student work samples showing varied approaches

content.title: The three EASE programs at a glance
content.text: EASE (Eduversal Analytical & Skills Evaluation) is an umbrella name, not a single test. Three evaluations run under it. They measure different things, are taken by different people and run on different schedules. So a school planning its year needs to put all three on the calendar separately.

content.title: The three EASE programs
rows: Student reasoning and literacy, independent of the curriculum
Student knowledge of subject content, following the Cambridge curriculum
Teacher subject knowledge and knowledge of how to teach the subject
Students in Grades 1-12, in the covered subjects. Grades 1-3 take Teacher-Paced Tests only. Performance-weighted subjects do not take it.
Teachers of Grades 1-12 in English, Mathematics, Physics, Chemistry, Biology and Integrated Science
Mathematical Reasoning, Science Literacy, English Reading
Subject Content Knowledge, Pedagogical Content Knowledge, General Pedagogical Knowledge
Twice a year for Grades 7-12 (once per semester); once a year for Grades 4-6, in Semester 2
Teacher-Paced Tests every 1-3 chapters, plus a Synchronized Test at the end of each semester
Where it sits in the year
Secondary: EASE Weeks 1 and 3 (mid-semester). The Semester 2 date may move earlier for grades with many exams. Primary (Grades 4-6): its own window at the start of Semester 2, outside the EASE Weeks
Teacher-Paced: any time within the planned window. Synchronized: EASE Weeks 2 and 4 (semester-end)
Window confirmed each year — see the network Assessment Schedule
No — formative, for professional development only

content.title: EASE Growth grade bands
rows: Band 4 — Advanced / AS and A Level

content.text: Each band takes one fixed-form package. Every student in the band sees the same paper at the same time. In 2026-27 (Version 1) there is one package per band. It sets a baseline and validates the items. Results are reported as a baseline, not as a growth score. In Phase 2, schools get equivalent Package A / Package B forms for the two Secondary sittings, and a formal semester-to-semester growth comparison. Both come once the packages have been technically linked.

content.title: EASE Weeks — and the difference between them
content.text:
There are four EASE Weeks in the school year, two in each semester. They are not the same, and the difference matters for the timetable.

EASE Weeks 1 and 3 fall in the middle of the semester. EASE Growth takes place in the first two periods of the assigned day. Normal lessons continue for the rest of the week.

EASE Weeks 2 and 4 fall at the end of each semester. Normal lessons stop, and the week is used for the Synchronized Tests. A school that treats all four weeks as normal teaching weeks will plan too much into the semester-end weeks.

EASE Academic is a test for teachers. Section 12.6 describes it, together with the other professional development support. It is named here only to complete the EASE umbrella. No part of it involves students, and none of its results go into any student record.
Purpose: To compare student performance with external standards, track growth over time and guide school improvement.

What: A standardized assessment across the whole Eduversal network. EASE Growth runs twice a year for Secondary (Grades 7-12), once in each semester. It runs once a year for Primary (Grades 4-6), in Semester 2.

Who: EASE Growth covers Grades 4-12 in four grade bands. EASE Assessment covers Grades 1-12 in the covered subjects. Performance-weighted subjects do not take it. What it measures: EASE Growth measures Mathematical Reasoning, Science Literacy and English Reading. EASE Assessment measures subject content from the taught curriculum.

items: Online platform (Latihan.id)

Scheduled windows: the four EASE Weeks, two in each semester. Weeks 1 and 3 are mid-semester (EASE Growth; lessons continue). Weeks 2 and 4 are at the end of the semester (Synchronized Tests; lessons stop). See the assessment calendar
Supervised by teachers (not high-stakes; held in classrooms)
Individual Student Reports: Show performance by skill/standard. In 2026-27 (Version 1), EASE Growth results are reported as a baseline, not as growth from a previous cycle
Class Reports: Combined data for the teacher (which objectives students have mastered and which need reteaching)
School Reports: Overall school performance, compared with the Eduversal network average
Eduversal Network Reports: Comparison across all 15+ partner schools
Teachers adjust their teaching based on the results
Schools identify professional development needs
Eduversal monitors network-wide quality
EASE Growth is NOT used for individual student grades. EASE Assessment (Common Assessment) results are graded and recorded as the Common Assessment Gradebook category
EASE administration schedules
Individual and aggregate EASE reports
PLC (Professional Learning Community) meeting notes that analyze EASE data and plan interventions
Quick results: For Common Assessment, Latihan.id reports once the test window closes. EASE Growth results are released only after the Growth Team's technical and data-quality checks
Full reports: EduNav > EASE > EASE Keys and Results

steps: Individual Student Reports: Results for each question, strengths/weaknesses, and comparison with the class/school/national average
Class Reports: High/low achievers, topic-by-topic evaluation, class strengths
Validity Reports: Analysis of question quality, used for continuous improvement
Topic Evaluation Reports: Performance in each subject compared with network schools
Certificates of Achievement: For the top 3 students in each subject (to motivate and recognize them)

items: School Management: Evaluate how well T&L (teaching and learning) works, find areas to improve and support accreditation
Teachers: Find the causes of underperformance and personalize teaching
Students: Understand their strengths/weaknesses and take ownership of their learning
Parents: Track progress, support learning at home
EASE reports (all five types, anonymized samples)
PLC meeting notes analyzing EASE data
Intervention plans based on EASE findings

content.text: What: Optional diagnostic tests from Cambridge for Grades 7-8 (Lower Secondary) in English, Math and Science. Purpose:

items: Check readiness for the next stage (especially IGCSE)
Identify strengths and gaps
Benchmark against international standards
Schools choose when to give them (usually once or twice per term). Results may be recorded in the Edunav Gradebook as formative evidence
Online or paper-based
Guide decisions about tier placement (e.g., Extended vs Core Math for IGCSE)
Guide intervention for students below the expected level
NOT high-stakes; not reported on transcript

content.text: Who: A sample of students in Grades 5, 8 and 11

items: Literacy and Numeracy (AKM - Asesmen Kompetensi Minimum)
Character (Survei Karakter - student wellbeing, P5 values)
Learning Environment (Survei Lingkungan Belajar - completed by teachers and the principal)
Centrally scheduled by the Ministry of Education (typically August-September)
Computer-based
School provides devices and proctors
School-level results only (not individual student grades)
Results published in Rapor Pendidikan (national education report card)
Comparison to national, provincial, and similar schools
School improvement planning (finding areas that need support)
National education policy and resource allocation
Results guide quality management discussions with the Yayasan and the Ministry
ANBK administration documentation
School-level results from the Rapor Pendidikan portal (the ministry website)
SIP (School Improvement Plan) reflecting ANBK findings

content.title: Tes Kemampuan Akademik (TKA) - Permendikdasmen No. 9/2025
content.text:
Permendikdasmen No. 9/2025 tentang Tes Kemampuan Akademik establishes the TKA (the national academic ability test). Peraturan Kepala BSKAP No. 45/2025 sets the assessment framework for SMA/MA and SMK/MAK. The TKA sits alongside the national assessment arrangements in this section. It also sits alongside Cambridge external examinations.

Before the TKA goes into the assessment calendar, schools should check which cohorts are in scope this year and how TKA results are used.

Sources: Permendikdasmen No. 9/2025 and Peraturan Kepala BSKAP No. 45/2025.

editorialNotes.title: Note on this block
editorialNotes.text: Authored by Eduversal, 2026-08-17. This block is new content, not transcribed source material. The corpus previously described EASE as a single subject-based exam and carried no statement of the three-program structure, the grade bands, or the EASE Week cycle. Content is derived from EASE Framework 26-27 (the comparison table at p.10 and the EASE Week description at p.11) and from EASE Growth: Overview 26-27 (grade bands and question counts; the Version 1 single-package design and the Phase 2 Package A / Package B plan, §4). Where the two sources overlap they agree; where only one carries a fact, it is cited individually above. Corrected 2026-09-29: this block previously described two equivalent papers, Form A in Semester 1 and Form B in Semester 2; the live EASE Growth: Overview 26-27 makes Version 1 a single fixed-form package per band, with Package A / Package B in Phase 2.

subsections.title: Reporting to Universities and Transcript Management

content.text: Purpose: To provide accurate and complete academic records for university admission, scholarships and transfers.

items: Student Information: Name, date of birth, student ID
School Information: School name, address, curriculum type (Cambridge + Indonesian)
Grades for all courses taken (usually Grades 9-12; some universities ask for earlier grades)
Course titles, credit hours (if applicable), grades, year taken
Separate sections for Cambridge subjects and Indonesian national subjects
Cambridge IGCSE, AS, A Level results (official grades from Cambridge)
ANBK participation noted (if applicable)
Calculated on a 4.0 scale (or other scale specified)
Weighted or unweighted (clearly indicated)
Class Rank (Optional): If the school ranks students
Graduation Date: Expected or actual
School Profile: A summary of the school curriculum, grading scale, available courses and university outcomes (this helps universities understand the grades in context)
Official transcripts: Sent in a sealed envelope with the school stamp, or sent electronically through a secure platform (Parchment, SLATE, etc.)
Unofficial transcripts: Students/parents may view them in EduNav. They are not valid for applications
Student submits transcript request form (online via EduNav or paper form)
The form gives: the recipient (university name/address), the delivery method (mail, electronic, pickup) and the number of copies
Processing time: 3-5 business days
A fee may apply (especially for urgent requests or international mailing)

content.text:
Predicted grades are a teacher's professional judgment of the grade a student is most likely to get in their final Cambridge examinations. Predicted grades are confidential. They are normally shared only with universities or scholarship bodies, as part of official school submissions.

They are based on evidence such as class assessments, mock examinations, coursework and the teacher's professional judgment.

Context: Many universities (especially in the UK, Australia and Canada) require predicted grades for students who apply before the final Cambridge results are available. Process:

steps: Teacher Assessment: The subject teacher predicts the grade the student is likely to get in the Cambridge external exam. The prediction is based on mock exams, coursework and classwork performance
Review: The Principal/Academic Coordinator checks the predictions for consistency
Letter: The school issues an official predicted grades letter on school letterhead, signed by the Principal
Confidentiality: Predictions are shared with universities but usually not with students/parents (to avoid pressure)

content.text: Accuracy Imperative: Predictions should be realistic. Over-predicting harms students, because a university may reject a student whose actual grades are much lower. It also damages the school's credibility.
Purpose: To give a qualitative assessment of the student's academic abilities, character and potential (this adds to grades/test scores). Process:

items: The student asks the teacher(s) and/or counselor for a recommendation (usually 2-3 letters are required by universities)
The student provides: a resume/CV, a draft personal statement, a university list and the deadline
How long and in what role they have known the student
Academic strengths and specific examples
Character qualities (curiosity, resilience, leadership, integrity)
Comparison to peers (if appropriate)
Endorsement of the student, and confidence in their success at university
The teacher sends the letter directly to the university (it is confidential; the student usually gives up the right to read it)
Students ask for letters at least 4-6 weeks before the deadline (earlier for popular teachers)
Transcript request logs
Predicted grade documentation
Recommendation letter request forms (a record of who asked, which teacher they asked and the deadline)
University outcomes data (where students were admitted; how predicted grades compare with actual grades, for continuous improvement)

subsections.title: Assessment Policy Review and Continuous Improvement

content.text: Purpose: Assessment practices change over time, based on research, student needs and stakeholder feedback.

Who: The Assessment Committee. The Academic Coordinator chairs it. Members are the School Principal, all Heads of Department and the Learning Support Coordinator where applicable. Eduversal joins the annual June review

items: Student achievement trends (are students improving from year to year?)
Assessment reliability and validity (are assessments measuring what they should? Are results consistent?)
Moderation effectiveness (are marks fair and consistent?)
Use of accommodations (are students getting the support they need?)
Teacher survey (workload, clarity of grading policies, moderation usefulness)
Student survey (fairness of assessments, clarity of expectations, usefulness of feedback)
Parent survey (communication of grades, understanding of reports)
Review educational research on assessment (new strategies, tools)
Benchmark against other schools (Eduversal network, international schools)

Update school rubrics and reporting formats if needed. Send any proposal to change the network grading scale or weighting profile to the Academic Board, with supporting evidence. Changes need written Academic Board approval
Add new assessment types (e.g., use more performance tasks)
Improve turnaround time for feedback
Strengthen moderation processes
Update Assessment Policy document
Tell staff, students and parents about the changes
Plan PD (professional development) sessions for teachers on assessment practices (designing good assessments, giving useful feedback, using data)
CIS/WASC accreditation self-study (Section 18) - assessment is a major focus area
Eduversal Supervisor visits (Section 2.17) - quality assurance includes assessment review
Assessment policy (current version with revision history)
Assessment committee meeting notes
Survey results (teachers, students, parents on assessment)
Professional development on assessment (attendance records, session materials)
Examples of assessment improvements made after the review

content.text: The Appraisal Program evaluates teaching quality through:

steps: Subject Specialist visits: Specialists observe classes across core subjects during the two Eduversal visits each year. Each observation is one lesson period of 35-45 min, or two periods in smaller subjects. These observations are formative only, with Glow / Grow / Go feedback. A teacher's F2 Classroom Observation score comes solely from the school's own appraisers (at least three formal observations per semester)

School Appraisal: An evaluation of the whole school across the five domains of the Eduversal School Appraisal Framework. The domains are Leadership & Governance, Teaching & Learning Quality, Curriculum & Academic Programs, Student Achievement & Learning Outcomes, and School Culture & Community. There are 33 aspects, rated Needs Intervention / Developing / Strong / Outstanding over two visits. See Section 17.8 for the full framework.
The Eduversal Appraisal Team carries it out every year
Results guide professional development planning (DTP)
Appraisal observation forms and rubrics
Post-appraisal meeting notes
Teacher improvement plans
Cross-reference: See Section 7.3 for teacher appraisal and classroom observation ownership, and Section 17.8 for the School Appraisal framework

editorialNotes.title: Correction history

Both were replaced: appraisal detail lives in Section 7.3 (teacher) and Section 17.8 (school), and the domain list now matches the current five-domain Eduversal School Appraisal Framework.

content.text: Comprehensive Assessment Documentation: All assessment data, records and reports are handled confidentially, in line with Indonesian data protection regulations and Eduversal policy. The Assessment Policy sets out the record-keeping requirements, storage procedures and retention periods. Policy and Procedures:

items: Assessment Policy (formative, summative, moderation, grading, reporting, integrity)
Academic Integrity Policy
Accommodations and Differentiation Guidelines
AI Usage Guidelines
Sample assessments (tests, rubrics, project descriptions) from each subject/grade
Assessment blueprints (alignment to standards)
Moderation cover sheets and protocols
Annual assessment calendar (all grades)
Exam schedules (Common Assessment windows and Synchronized Tests from the EASE Schedule, Cambridge mocks, external exams)
EASE reports (individual, class, school, network)
Cambridge results (Checkpoint, IGCSE, AS/A Level) - past 3 years
ANBK results (school-level)
PLC meeting notes with data analysis
Report card templates (Cambridge subjects, Indonesian subjects, Profil Pelajar Pancasila, character)
Sample report cards (redacted for privacy)
Parent-Teacher Conference schedules and notes
Transcripts (official and unofficial formats)
Academic Integrity Incident Reports (anonymized summaries)
Plagiarism detection reports (Turnitin summaries)
Student integrity pledges
IEP/accommodation documentation
Access arrangement approvals (Cambridge)
Implementation logs
Assessment-focused PD session materials
Teacher training on rubrics, moderation, feedback
Cambridge Assessment Standards: Internal and external moderation procedures; coursework integrity; secure exam administration; fair and valid assessment
Indonesian Curriculum Standards: Assessment aligned to Capaian Pembelajaran (CP); Profil Pelajar Pancasila competency assessment; reporting requirements
CIS Standards: Teaching & Assessing for Learning (assessment guides teaching; it is valid and reliable, fair and ethical, and clearly communicated)
WASC Category B: Curriculum, Instruction, and Assessment (Criterion B3 - assessment practices are valid, reliable and equitable; results are used to improve learning)
Eduversal SLOs (Student Learning Outcomes): Assessment measures progress toward SLOs, and SLO-linked reports go to parents
